fragments.text: Nature has built almost everything you
can imagine. Animals that can survive
being frozen, boiled, and thrown into
outer space. Fish that generate their
own electricity. Lizards that literally
shoot blood out of their eyes. Jellyfish
that technically never have to die. And
octopuses that taste everything they
touch with their arms. But there is one
creature nature simply refused to build.
So humans invented it anyway. We call it
a dragon. When you picture a dragon, you
probably see the western version. A
giant winged reptile breathing fire. But
look at the monsters dreamed up that
never touched each other. A serpent
dragon winding through ancient China. A
feathered snake god in the Americas. A
rainbow serpent in Australia. A
fire-breathing lizard in medieval
Europe. The details shift from place to
place. Underneath though, people kept
reaching for the same handful of parts.
The scales and bulk of a giant reptile.
The coiling body of a snake. And the raw
menace of a great predator. [music] The
same monster invented from scratch on
continent after continent. Evolution had
4 billion years and a whole planet to
work with. It came close to a dragon
more than once. So why did it never
happen? And stranger still, why did
humans invent it anyway? That answer
isn't about the animals at all. It's
about you. Start with the fire because
that's the part that sounds the most
impossible. And weirdly, it's the part
nature got closest to. There's an insect
called the bombardier beetle. When
something threatens it, it mixes two
chemicals, hydrogen peroxide and a
compound called hydroquinone, inside a
tiny armored chamber in its abdomen. The
reaction is so violent, it heats the
liquid to nearly 212° Fahrenheit, the
temperature of boiling water, and blasts
it out the back with a sound like a pop
gun. It can swivel the tip of its
abdomen to aim and fire that spray
around 20 times in a row at whatever's
trying to eat it. That is the closest
thing to a flamethrower in the entire
animal kingdom. And it still isn't fire.
It's boiling spray, not [music] a flame.
In fact, no animal we know of ever
evolved a way to set something on fire.
So already the single most famous dragon
feature is the one nature flatly refused
to sign off on. Now, the body. We
actually have an animal we named after
the myth itself, the Komodo dragon. It's
the largest lizard alive today, about 10
ft long, the length of a small car with
a venomous bite that can take down prey
far bigger than itself. But, the Komodo
is a leftover. Its ancestors were much
worse. Until around 50,000 years ago,
Australia was home to a monitor lizard
called Megalania. It could reach
anywhere from 18 ft to even 23 ft long.
A venomous reptile longer than a car,
and the first humans who reached
Australia very likely shared the land
with it. That's not a dragon, but it's a
real reptile big enough to pass for one.
Then, there's flight. And there is a
lizard alive right now that flies, sort
of. It's called [music] Draco, and it
lives in the forests of Southeast Asia.
Those wings didn't come from nowhere. It
took the ribs inside its own chest,
stretched them way out to the sides, and
pulled a flap of skin across them like a
folding fan. It leaps off a tree, those
ribs open, and glides as far as 200 ft
to the next trunk. That's 2/3 of a
football field. Draco didn't grow new
limbs. It just built a wing out of the
bones it already had. In the last days
of the dinosaurs, around 68 million
years ago, the sky belonged to
Quetzalcoatlus, a flying reptile with a
36-ft wingspan, as tall as a giraffe
when it folded up and stood on the
ground, weighing somewhere near 550 lb,
a living creature the size of a small
plane that got into the air by vaulting
off its own arms like a pole vaulter,
and then actually flew. Yes, a
giraffe-sized reptile really did pole
vault into the sky. So, every piece of a
dragon already exists, or used to exist.
Nature just never let one animal have
them all at once. And that isn't bad
luck. There are hard reasons. The first
one is hiding in plain sight, right
there on the Welsh flag. A classic
Western dragon has four legs and two
wings. Add those up, and you get six
limbs. Every animal with a backbone,
you, a bird, a snake, a whale, a
Tyrannosaurus, traces back to the same
four-limbed fish that first crawled out
of the water. Four limbs. That's the
starting kit. And nobody since has ever
been handed a spare pair. When a bird
flies, it isn't using extra arms. Its
wings are its arms. Bats did the same
thing. So did those giant pterosaurs. To
grow wings, a backbone animal has to
give up its front legs and rebuild them
into the wings. You can have arms or you
can have wings. Nature does not hand out
both. That is exactly why poor Draco had
to build its glider out of rib bones.
The ribs were the only spare parts lying
around. A four-legged, two-winged dragon
needs a body plan no backbone animal has
ever had. It would have to break a
four-limbed rule that has held since the
first of them crawled onto land more
than 350 million years ago. The second
reason is pure size. Make [music] any
animal twice as long and it becomes
roughly eight times as heavy, but its
bones and muscles only get about four
times as strong. Scale a creature up far
enough and its own weight begins to
crush it from the inside.
Quetzalcoatlus, that giraffe-sized
flyer, was already scraping against the
absolute ceiling for how big a thing can
get and still haul itself off the
ground. A dragon the size of a house
with wings isn't just a bigger
Quetzalcoatlus. It's a pile of snapped
bones that never leaves the cliff edge.
And the third reason loops right back to
the fire. Flying is the most
metabolically expensive thing an animal
can do. It burns oxygen and energy at a
rate that shoves a body to its physical
limit just to stay in the air. There is
nothing left in that budget to also run
a furnace in your chest. And evolution
never sits down to design an animal
towards some final goal. It just tinkers
with whatever already exists, one tiny
accidental step at a time. No chain of
those tiny steps ever stumbled into a
winged, six-limbed, self-igniting
reptile. The dragon isn't blocked by one
rule. It's blocked by all of them at
once, stacked on top of each other. If a
dragon is that impossible, that
thoroughly forbidden by both biology and
physics, then why on earth did everyone
draw one? There are two leading ideas.
The first idea is bones. Long before
anyone on the planet knew what a
dinosaur was, people were digging
enormous fossils out of the ground and
trying to make sense of them. A
historian at Stanford named Adrienne
Mayor traced one of these cases
directly. Thousands of years ago,
Scythian gold miners crossing the Gobi
Desert kept unearthing the skeletons of
a beaked, four-legged creature we now
call Protoceratops. They had [music]
absolutely no concept of an extinct
animal, so they rebuilt those bones in
their minds into a guardian beast, and
that became the legend of the Griffin.
It happened on the other side of the
world, too. In China, the fossils people
dug up and ground into medicine were
called, quite literally, dragon bones.
All over the planet, humans found giant,
impossible skeletons in the dirt and
invented monsters to explain them. The
second idea is darker, and it's about
what's inside your own head. There's an
anthropologist named David E. Jones who
noticed something strange about monkeys.
Vervet monkeys have three [music]
separate alarm calls, three specific
screams for three specific killers. One
warns the troop about big cats on the
ground. Another means an eagle is diving
in from above. The last one means snake.
Those three animals, the cat, the eagle,
and the snake, are the exact predators
that hunted primates like us for
millions upon millions of years. Jones's
idea is that the fear of all three got
burned so deep into our brains that over
time they melted together into one
single image. Take the fangs and raking
claws of the great cat, [music] bolt on
the wings and the killing dive of the
eagle, wrap the whole thing in the long,
coiling, scaled body of the snake. Put
those three together and you have just
built a dragon. This one is only a
theory, and a hotly argued one. You
can't dig an instinct out of the ground,
and plenty of serious researchers think
it reaches way too far, but [music] it
explains the thing the fossils can't.
Not just why we invented a monster, why
we kept inventing this exact one. The
same parts bolted together the same way
on every continent by people who had
never once spoken to each other. The
reason nature never built a dragon is
that the dragon was never actually an
animal. Every single piece of it is
real. The fire is a beetle's boiling
spray. The size was a monitor lizard
hunting across Australia. Real
pterosaurs owned the wings. And the fear
underneath all of it is a memory far
older than our whole species. But the
assembly never once happened out in the
wild. It happened in here. The dragon is
the shape your ancestors nightmares took
when every predator that ever wanted to
eat them got stitched together into a
single body. Nature never made a dragon,
but we did out of everything that used
to hunt us in the dark.
